entries.gist: Digital patient record, shared across providers
entries.description: A digital version of a patient's medical history designed to be shared across different healthcare providers and settings, not just one practice — the interoperable successor to the older EMR.
entries.note: EHR software is normally bought off the shelf. Epic and Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) dominate the US hospital market, with MEDITECH a strong third, especially in community hospitals.
entries._source: Web research: EHR vendor market share, Sept 2026

entries.gist: Digital chart within a single practice
entries.description: A digital version of the paper chart within one practice or organisation. The record generally isn't designed to be shared outside that practice, which is the main thing that distinguishes it from an EHR.
entries.note: EMR is the older term historically; the industry has largely moved on to interoperable EHR systems, though the two words are still often used interchangeably in casual conversation.

entries.fullName: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
entries.gist: US law protecting patient data privacy
entries.description: US federal law setting standards for protecting patient health information and giving patients rights over their own records. Breaching it can carry serious fines, so it comes up constantly in any US-facing health IT or data project.

entries.gist: Patient data protected under privacy law
entries.description: Any patient information that could identify an individual and relates to their health, treatment or payment for care. Handling PHI correctly is what HIPAA compliance is actually about in practice.

entries.gist: US regulator for drugs and medical devices
entries.description: The US government agency responsible for approving new drugs and medical devices before they can be sold, and for regulating their safety afterwards. Its decisions influence pharma and med-tech timelines worldwide, not just in the US.

entries.gist: US agency running Medicare and Medicaid
entries.description: The US federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid and sets many of the billing and quality rules the rest of the US healthcare industry follows. Not to be confused with a content management system — a different CMS entirely, in IT.

entries.gist: Getting paid for care that was delivered
entries.description: The end-to-end process of billing for healthcare services — from checking a patient's insurance eligibility, through coding and submitting claims, to collecting payment. A major cost centre for any provider.
entries.note: RCM software is usually bought rather than built — Epic, Oracle Health, Waystar and R1 RCM are common vendors — and the work itself is often outsourced entirely to a specialist billing company.

entries.gist: Alerts and guidance built into clinical software
entries.description: Software features that give clinicians guidance at the point of care — flagging a drug interaction, suggesting a diagnosis, or reminding them of a guideline.
entries.note: Like FLISR inside an ADMS, CDS is typically a feature bundled inside an EHR (Epic, Oracle Health, etc.) rather than something bought as its own separate system.

entries.description: A company that sits between drug manufacturers, insurers and pharmacies, negotiating prices and deciding which drugs an insurance plan will cover. A major, and often controversial, player in US drug pricing.

entries.gist: Insurance plan with a limited provider network
entries.description: A health insurance plan that only covers care from a specific network of doctors and hospitals, usually via a primary care gatekeeper who refers patients to specialists. Typically cheaper than plans with a wider network.

entries.gist: Providers sharing responsibility for cost and quality
entries.description: A group of doctors, hospitals and other providers who voluntarily coordinate care for a defined patient population and share in any savings — or losses — against a cost target, rewarding quality over volume of care.
The coding system used to classify diagnoses and health conditions for billing, statistics and research — every diagnosis on a claim or medical record maps to an ICD-10 code.
entries.note: Maintained by the World Health Organization. A successor, ICD-11, was published in 2019, but adoption has been slow — the US and many other countries were still on ICD-10 as of the most recent reporting.
entries._source: Web research: ICD-11 adoption status, Sept 2026
